question.prompt:
Points \(A,\) \(B,\) \(C\) and \(D\) are midpoints of the sides of the larger square. If the larger square has area \(60,\) what is the area of the smaller square?

[Figure 1](figures/2006_AMC_8_Q05_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
The midpoints suggest dividing the larger square into equal parts. Draw \(AC\) and \(BD\). These segments divide the larger square into four equal squares, each with side length half the original side length.

Each side of \(ABCD\) is a diagonal of one of these four squares. The triangle on either side of that diagonal has the same base and height as its square, so the triangle area formula gives half the square's area. Exactly one of these two triangles lies inside \(ABCD\).

Thus \(ABCD\) contains half of each of the four parts, so its area is
\[
60\div2=\boxed{30}
\]
square units, choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
solutions.title: Divide into equal parts
